stimuli.text: Initial-rate data for A + B → products:
A student heats 5.9 g of $$\ce{CaCO3(s)}$$, which decomposes completely: $$\ce{CaCO3(s) -> CaO(s) + CO2(g)}$$. The $$\ce{CO2}$$ is collected at 316 K and 1 atm.
The decomposition of compound X was monitored at constant temperature.
A student titrates 33.0 mL of 0.12 M weak monoprotic acid HA (Ka = 1.8 \times 10^{-5}) with 0.15 M NaOH.
4.8 g of $$\ce{KNO3}$$ dissolves in 108 g of water in a coffee-cup calorimeter. The temperature falls by 4.9 °C. Assume the solution's specific heat is 4.18 J/(g·°C).

A galvanic cell is made of a Mg electrode in 1.0 M $$\ce{Mg^{2+}}$$ and a Ni electrode in 1.0 M $$\ce{Ni^{2+}}$$. Standard reduction potentials: $$\ce{Mg^{2+} + 2e- -> Mg}$$ E° = -2.37 V; $$\ce{Ni^{2+} + 2e- -> Ni}$$ E° = -0.25 V.
The photoelectron spectra of C (Z = 6) and N (Z = 7) are compared.

questions.stem: A reaction has a theoretical yield of 30.9 g. The actual yield is 20.1 g. What is the percent yield?
What is the pH of a 0.25 M solution of $$\ce{Ca(OH)2}$$ at 25 °C?

options.why: Each formula unit releases two OH⁻.
Correct. Strong base: [OH⁻] = 2 × 0.25 M; pH = 14 − pOH.
That is the pOH; subtract from 14.
Strong acids and bases ionize completely; no equilibrium is needed.

questions.stem: What is the oxidation number of Fe in $$\ce{Fe2O3}$$?

options.why: Make the oxidation numbers add up to the overall charge.
Make the oxidation numbers add up to the overall charge.
Make the oxidation numbers add up to the overall charge.
Correct. The oxidation numbers must sum to the species' overall charge (O usually −2, H usually +1).

questions.stem: What is the pressure of 2.85 mol of gas in a 31 L container at 412 K?

options.why: With L and atm, use R = 0.08206.

questions.stem: Why does temperature remain constant while ice melts?

options.text: Added energy overcomes intermolecular forces rather than increasing kinetic energy
options.why: Correct. Phase changes occur at constant temperature.

options.text: Covalent bonds in water are breaking
options.why: Melting does not break covalent bonds.

questions.explanation: Phase changes occur at constant temperature.

questions.stem: How many formula units or molecules are in 19 g of $$\ce{CuSO4}$$?

options.why: Correct. Convert grams to moles, then multiply by Avogadro's number.

questions.stem: Which compound has the greater lattice energy, $$\ce{LiF}$$ or $$\ce{MgF2}$$?

options.text: $$\ce{LiF}$$, because it has more atoms per formula unit
options.why: Number of atoms does not determine lattice energy.

options.text: $$\ce{MgF2}$$, because its ions have larger charges
options.why: Correct. By Coulomb's law, attraction increases with the product of the ion charges.

options.text: They are equal because both are ionic
$$\ce{LiF}$$, because its ions have larger charges

questions.explanation: MgF2 has ion charges 2 and 1; LiF has 1 and 1.

questions.stem: A reaction has a theoretical yield of 17 g. The actual yield is 14.6 g. What is the percent yield?
Which bond is the most polar?

options.why: Correct. It has the largest electronegativity difference (1.8).

questions.stem: On a reaction energy profile, the reactants are at 113 kJ/mol, the transition state at 175 kJ/mol and the products at 127 kJ/mol. What is the activation energy of the reverse reaction?

options.why: Correct. Reverse Ea = transition state − products.
Measure from the correct starting point.

questions.explanation: Forward Ea = 62, ΔH = 14, reverse Ea = 48 kJ/mol.

questions.stem: What volume does 1.9 mol of gas occupy at 17.5 atm and 337 K?

options.why: Use R = 0.08206 with atm and L.
22.4 L/mol applies only at 0 °C and 1 atm.

questions.stem: How does a catalyst increase the rate of a reaction?

options.text: It provides a pathway with a lower activation energy
options.why: Correct. The reaction goes by a different mechanism.

questions.explanation: The reaction goes by a different mechanism.

questions.stem: A gas mixture contains 0.4 mol N₂, 0.5 mol O₂ and 0.6 mol Ar at a total pressure of 1.9 atm. What is the partial pressure of N₂?

options.why: The gases are not present in equal amounts.
Use the mole fraction, not moles.

questions.stem: What is the molarity of a solution made by dissolving 0.133 mol of solute in enough water to make 707 mL of solution?
Under which conditions does a real gas deviate most from ideal behavior?

options.why: Correct. Particle volume and attractions matter most.

questions.explanation: Particle volume and attractions matter most.

questions.stem: A first-order reaction has a half-life of 10 min. Starting at 15.5 M, what is the concentration after 50 min?

options.why: Each half-life halves the concentration; it is not divided by 2n.

questions.stem: What is the molarity of a solution made by dissolving 0.119 mol of solute in enough water to make 946 mL of solution?
A gas mixture contains 0.5 mol N₂, 0.2 mol O₂ and 0.1 mol Ar at a total pressure of 4.9 atm. What is the partial pressure of N₂?

options.why: The gases are not present in equal amounts.
Use the mole fraction, not moles.

questions.stem: Is $$\ce{SiH4}$$ polar or nonpolar, and why?

options.why: Containing H does not make a molecule polar.

options.text: Nonpolar, because its bond dipoles cancel by symmetry
Polar, because its bond dipoles do not cancel
options.why: Consider the molecule's shape, not only its bonds.

options.text: Polar, because all its bonds are polar
options.why: Polarity depends on both bond polarity and geometry.

questions.explanation: SiH4 is tetrahedral; the dipoles cancel.

questions.stem: A solution has an absorbance of 0.926 in a 2 cm cuvette. The molar absorptivity is 178 M⁻¹cm⁻¹. What is the concentration?
For $$\ce{A(g) + B(g) <=> 2C(g)}$$, K = 5.6. A mixture has [A] = 0.1 M, [B] = 0.4 M and [C] = 0.3 M. In which direction will the reaction proceed?

options.text: It proceeds forward, toward products, because Q = 2.25
options.why: Correct. Q = [C]²/([A][B]) = 2.25, which is less than K.

options.text: It is at equilibrium, because Q = K
It proceeds forward, toward products, because Q = 7.5
It proceeds in reverse, toward reactants, because Q = 2.25
options.why: If Q is less than K, the reaction proceeds forward.

questions.stem: A reaction has K = 28. What is K for the reaction reversed and multiplied by 2?

options.why: Multiplying by n raises K to the nth power.
K is raised to a power, not multiplied.
Correct. Reverse → 1/K; multiply by n → Kⁿ.

questions.stem: A first-order reaction has a rate constant of 0.0408 min⁻¹. What is its half-life?
What is the energy of a photon with a wavelength of 306 nm?

options.why: Correct. E = hc/λ, with λ in meters.

questions.stem: Use the bond enthalpies to estimate ΔH for $$\ce{H2 + Br2 -> 2HBr}$$.

options.why: Correct. ΔH ≈ Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds formed).
Bonds formed release energy: subtract them.
Multiply each bond energy by the number of bonds.
Broken minus formed, not formed minus broken.

questions.stem: A 44.8 mL sample of $$\ce{H2SO4}$$ is titrated to the equivalence point with 14.1 mL of 0.273 M NaOH. What is the concentration of the acid?

options.why: Correct. Each H₂SO₄ reacts with two OH⁻, so divide the moles of NaOH by 2.

questions.stem: A weak acid HA has pKa = 10.7. In a solution at pH 11.2, which statement is correct?

options.why: Correct. Above the pKa, the deprotonated form dominates.

questions.stem: A reaction has K = 2 × 10⁻¹². At equilibrium:

options.text: Reactant and product concentrations are equal

questions.stem: A solid melts at 1,710 °C, is very hard and does not conduct electricity. It is most likely:

options.why: Molecular solids melt at low temperatures.

options.text: An ionic solid that conducts as a solid
options.why: Ionic solids do not conduct as solids.

questions.stem: Samples of $$\ce{He}$$, $$\ce{O2}$$, $$\ce{CH4}$$, $$\ce{N2}$$ are all at the same temperature. Which has the highest average molecular speed?

options.why: Correct. At the same temperature, average kinetic energy is equal, so the lightest gas moves fastest.
N2 has a larger molar mass (28 g/mol).
CH4 has a larger molar mass (16 g/mol).
O2 has a larger molar mass (32 g/mol).

questions.explanation: Molar masses: He 4, O2 32, CH4 16, N2 28.

questions.stem: For $$\ce{A(g) + B(g) <=> 2C(g)}$$, K = 4.4. A mixture has [A] = 0.6 M, [B] = 0.3 M and [C] = 0.8 M. In which direction will the reaction proceed?

options.text: It is at equilibrium, because Q = K
It proceeds forward, toward products, because Q = 4.44
It proceeds forward, toward products, because Q = 3.56
options.why: Correct. Q = [C]²/([A][B]) = 3.56, which is less than K.

options.text: It proceeds in reverse, toward reactants, because Q = 3.56
options.why: If Q is less than K, the reaction proceeds forward.

questions.stem: At 298 K, ΔG° for a reaction is -8 kJ/mol. What is K?

options.why: Correct. K = e^(−ΔG°/RT), with ΔG° in J/mol and R = 8.314.

questions.explanation: ln K = 3.23; K = 25.3. Negative ΔG°: K greater than 1.

questions.stem: What is the mass percent of H in $$\ce{H2SO4}$$?

options.why: There are 2 atoms of H in the formula.
Use masses, not numbers of atoms.
That is the percent of the other elements.

questions.stem: For a reaction, ΔH° = 134 kJ/mol and ΔS° = 110 J/(mol·K). What is ΔG° at 799 K, and is the reaction favorable?

options.why: Correct. ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, with ΔS in kJ/(mol·K).
Convert ΔS from J to kJ.

questions.stem: The first four ionization energies of an element are 683, 4098, 6680, 11156 kJ/mol. In which group of the periodic table is the element most likely found?

options.why: Locate the largest jump between successive ionization energies.
Locate the largest jump between successive ionization energies.
Locate the largest jump between successive ionization energies.
Correct. The large jump comes after removing 1 electron, so it has 1 valence electron.

questions.explanation: The big jump marks the start of removing core electrons.

questions.stem: Two buffers have the same pH, but buffer X has ten times the concentration of each component. Which is true?

options.text: Buffer X has a greater buffer capacity
options.why: Correct. More acid and base are available to react.

options.text: Buffer X cannot resist pH changes
Buffer X has a lower pH
options.why: The ratio, and pH, are the same.

questions.explanation: More acid and base are available to react.

questions.stem: 126 g of water at 85 °C is mixed with 185 g of water at 5 °C in an insulated container. What is the final temperature?

options.why: Pair each mass with its own temperature.
Correct. Heat lost = heat gained; for water alone, a mass-weighted average.

questions.stem: A weak acid HA has pKa = 7.6. In a solution at pH 9.9, which statement is correct?

options.why: Correct. Above the pKa, the deprotonated form dominates.

questions.stem: Calculate ΔH° for $$\ce{2SO2 + O2 -> 2SO3}$$. (ΔH°f of O₂ is 0.)

options.why: Multiply each ΔH°f by its coefficient.
Correct. Σ n ΔH°f(products) − Σ n ΔH°f(reactants).

questions.stem: What is the pH of a 0.05 M solution of hypochlorous acid (Ka = 3 \times 10^{-8})?

options.why: A weak acid does not ionize completely.
Correct. Solve Ka = x²/(C − x) for x = [H₃O⁺].

questions.stem: A buffer contains 0.43 mol of a weak acid HA (pKa 4.74) and 0.47 mol of its conjugate base A⁻. Then 0.04 mol of NaOH is added. What is the pH?

options.why: Update moles after the added acid or base reacts.
Correct. First react: OH⁻ converts HA to A⁻. Then pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]).

questions.stem: What is the energy of a photon with a wavelength of 448 nm?

options.why: Correct. E = hc/λ, with λ in meters.

questions.stem: For $$\ce{4NH3 + 5O2 -> 4NO + 6H2O}$$, $$\ce{O2}$$ is consumed at 0.85 M/s. At what rate does $$\ce{H2O}$$ form?

options.why: Divide by the reactant's coefficient too.
Correct. Multiply by the coefficient ratio 6/5.

questions.stem: Steel is harder than pure iron because:

options.text: Small carbon atoms in the gaps (interstitial alloy) hinder layers of iron atoms from sliding
Carbon replaces iron atoms of the same size

questions.stem: Which is the ground-state electron configuration of potassium (K, Z = 19)?

options.why: Correct. Fill orbitals in order until 19 electrons are placed.

questions.stem: Which is a physical change?

options.why: Correct. Only intermolecular forces are overcome.

questions.stem: For the galvanic cell made from these half-cells, what is ΔG°? (F = 96,485 C/mol)

options.why: ΔG° is negative for a positive E°.
Correct. ΔG° = −nFE° with n = 2 electrons transferred and E° = 1.05 V.

questions.stem: How many valence electrons are shown in the Lewis structure of $$\ce{H2O}$$?

options.why: Correct. Sum the valence electrons of all atoms, then add one per negative charge (subtract one per positive charge).

questions.stem: Reaction 1 has ΔH₁ = -162 kJ and reaction 2 has ΔH₂ = -3 kJ. A target reaction is obtained by doubling reaction 1 and adding reaction 2. What is ΔH for the target reaction?

options.why: Correct. Reverse → change sign; multiply → multiply ΔH; then add.
Enthalpies add; they do not multiply.
Reversing changes the sign of ΔH₂.

questions.stem: How can an unfavorable reaction (ΔG positive) be made to occur?

options.text: By coupling it to a favorable reaction so the total ΔG is negative

questions.stem: A photoelectron spectrum shows 3 peaks. From highest to lowest binding energy, their relative heights are 2 : 2 : 1. Which element is it?

options.why: Correct. The peaks correspond to $$1s^{2}\,2s^{2}\,2p^{1}$$, which has 5 electrons.

questions.stem: For $$\ce{H2(g) + I2(g) <=> 2HI(g)}$$, initial [H₂] = 1.3 M and [I₂] = 1.8 M, with no HI. At equilibrium, [HI] = 0.62 M. What is K?
A compound (butane) is 82.7% C, 17.3% H by mass. What is its empirical formula?

options.why: That is the molecular formula; reduce to the simplest ratio.
Correct. Convert each percent (in 100 g) to moles and divide by the smallest.

questions.explanation: The mole ratio reduces to C2H5; the molecular formula is C4H10.

questions.stem: The Ksp of $$\ce{Mg(OH)2}$$ is 5.6 \times 10^{-12}. What is its molar solubility in pure water?
A buffer contains 0.38 mol of a weak acid HA (pKa 4.74) and 0.42 mol of A⁻. What is its pH?
When a reaction involving 0.062 mol of limiting reactant occurs in 152 g of solution (c = 4.18 J/(g·°C)), the temperature falls by 11.5 °C. What is ΔH for the reaction?

options.why: Correct. q(solution) = mcΔT = 7310 J; q(reaction) = −q(solution); divide by moles.
A temperature rise means the reaction is exothermic (negative ΔH).
Divide by the moles of reactant.

questions.stem: A weak acid (pKa 4.87) is titrated with NaOH; the equivalence point is reached at 6.73 mL. What is the pH after 3.37 mL of NaOH has been added?

options.why: That is only for strong acid–strong base equivalence.
Correct. At the half-equivalence point, [HA] = [A⁻], so pH = pKa.

questions.stem: For $$\ce{C3H8 + 5O2 -> 3CO2 + 4H2O}$$, 39 g of $$\ce{C3H8}$$ reacts with 19 g of $$\ce{O2}$$. What mass of $$\ce{CO2}$$ can form?

options.why: Not all of both reactants reacts.
Apply the mole ratio from the equation.
Correct. O2 is the limiting reactant.
Use the limiting reactant, which gives less product.

questions.stem: What is the rate law?

options.why: Compare trials where only one concentration changes.
Correct. Doubling [A] multiplies the rate by 4; doubling [B] multiplies it by 1.
Recheck how the rate changes when [B] doubles.
Orders are found from the data, not from coefficients.

questions.explanation: Trials 1→2: rate ×4, so order 2 in A. Trials 1→3: rate ×1, so order 0 in B.

questions.stem: A reaction has ΔG° = −50 kJ/mol but does not occur noticeably at room temperature. The best explanation is:

options.text: It has a high activation energy, so it is under kinetic control
options.why: Correct. Favorable is not the same as fast.
Negative ΔG° means K greater than 1.

questions.explanation: Favorable is not the same as fast.

parts.prompt: Calculate the number of moles of CO₂ produced.

rubric.criterion: Correct moles using molar mass 100.09 g/mol and the 1:1 ratio.

parts.prompt: Calculate the volume of CO₂ expected.
The student measures 1.406 L of gas. Calculate the percent yield, and give one experimental reason the yield could be less than 100%.

rubric.example: Incomplete decomposition (not heated long enough) or gas leaking from the apparatus.

parts.prompt: Draw (describe) a complete Lewis diagram for CO₂, and identify its molecular geometry and the hybridization of carbon.

rubric.example: O=C=O with two lone pairs on each O (16 valence electrons).

parts.prompt: Explain why CO₂ is nonpolar even though C=O bonds are polar.

rubric.criterion: Linear symmetry makes the bond dipoles cancel.

parts.prompt: CaO is an ionic solid. Explain, using Coulomb's law, why CaO has a higher melting point than KCl.

rubric.criterion: Larger ion charges in CaO (2+/2−) than in KCl (1+/1−).
Greater electrostatic attraction (and smaller ions) means more energy is needed to separate the ions.

parts.prompt: Calculate the average rate of disappearance of X between 0 and 20 s.
Determine the order of the reaction with respect to X. Justify your answer using the data.

rubric.example: Equal time intervals give equal changes in 1/[X].

parts.prompt: Write the rate law and determine the rate constant, with units.
Calculate the half-life of the reaction (for the initial concentration).
A proposed mechanism has a slow first step: 2X → X₂. Is the mechanism consistent with the rate law? Explain.

rubric.criterion: Yes; the slow step's elementary rate law matches the observed rate law.

parts.prompt: A catalyst is added. Explain its effect on the rate and on the rate constant, using activation energy.

rubric.example: The catalyst provides a new pathway.

rubric.criterion: Lower activation energy means a larger fraction of collisions are successful.

parts.prompt: Write the net ionic equation for the titration reaction.
Calculate the initial pH of the acid solution.

rubric.criterion: Ka expression set up with x = [H₃O⁺].

parts.prompt: Calculate the volume of NaOH needed to reach the equivalence point.
What is the pH at the half-equivalence point? Justify.
Calculate the pH at the equivalence point.

rubric.criterion: Uses Kb = Kw/Ka and the diluted [A⁻].

parts.prompt: Choose an appropriate indicator from: methyl orange (pKa 3.7), bromothymol blue (pKa 7.0), phenolphthalein (pKa 9.3). Justify.

rubric.criterion: Indicator whose pKa is closest to the equivalence pH.

parts.prompt: Explain why the solution at the half-equivalence point resists pH change when a small amount of HCl is added.

rubric.criterion: A⁻ reacts with added H⁺ to form HA (buffer).
rubric.example: A⁻ + H₃O⁺ → HA + H₂O, so the ratio [A⁻]/[HA] changes only slightly.

parts.prompt: Is the dissolution endothermic or exothermic? Justify.

rubric.example: Endothermic: the solution cooled, so energy was absorbed.

parts.prompt: Calculate the heat absorbed or released by the solution.
Calculate ΔH of dissolution in kJ/mol.
If some heat escaped to the surroundings, would the magnitude of the calculated ΔH be too large or too small? Explain.

rubric.criterion: Too small, because the measured temperature change is smaller than the true change.

parts.prompt: Write the balanced net ionic equation for the cell reaction.
Calculate E°cell.
Calculate ΔG° for the cell reaction.
The concentration of Mg²⁺ is increased to 2.0 M. Predict the effect on the cell potential and justify.

rubric.criterion: E decreases because Q increases (a product's concentration rises).
rubric.example: Q greater than 1 → E less than E°.

questions.title: Solubility of a slightly soluble salt

parts.prompt: Write the Ksp expression.
Calculate the molar solubility in pure water.
Calculate the molar solubility in a solution containing 0.1 M OH⁻ (from a soluble salt).
Explain how lowering the pH affects the solubility.

rubric.criterion: Correct reasoning about whether the anion is basic.
rubric.example: Solubility increases: H⁺ reacts with OH⁻ (a base), shifting the equilibrium toward dissolving.

parts.prompt: Write the electron configuration of N.
Explain why the 1s peak of N has a higher binding energy than the 1s peak of C.

rubric.criterion: N has more protons, so 1s electrons are attracted more strongly (Coulomb's law).

parts.prompt: Describe one difference in the number or relative height of peaks between the two spectra.

rubric.criterion: A valid difference based on configurations.
rubric.example: N has one more electron, so its outermost peak is taller or an extra peak appears.

parts.prompt: Which element has the larger atomic radius? Justify using Coulomb's law.

rubric.criterion: C: fewer protons with similar shielding, so valence electrons are held less tightly.
rubric.example: Same period; effective nuclear charge increases across.
